faq: What data do you need to plan a roadmap?
Whatever you have: feedback messages, support emails, sign-up numbers or notes from user calls. If you have little, we say so and plan around the questions you still need to answer.
Is this the same as product scoping?
No. Scoping defines a first version before it exists. Roadmap planning is for products that are already live or about to be, and decides the order of improvements using real user signals.
Will you commit to a delivery date for each item?
We give effort estimates as ranges and flag the risks, not promises. Dates depend on your team's capacity. If we build the work, we confirm timing in a written fixed price quote.
Which format do I receive the roadmap in?
A shareable page or document, plus a spreadsheet version if you prefer to track it yourself. It uses plain labels, so teammates and investors can read it without a briefing.

desc:
Post-launch product roadmap planning decides what your live SaaS product should build next, and what to leave out. Ecom Swift LLC reviews your feedback, usage and goals, then writes a clear, ordered roadmap with reasons and rough effort for every item.

## What is a post-launch product roadmap?

A product roadmap is an ordered plan of what a team intends to build over the coming months, grouped into time horizons such as now, next and later. A post-launch roadmap is written after real users exist, so it draws on evidence: what they asked for, where they get stuck and what they actually use.

It is a statement of priorities and reasons, not a contract. Items can move as you learn, which is why each one carries its reasoning.

## Why a live product creates too many urgent ideas

After launch, requests arrive from every direction: customers, partners, investors and your own list of ideas. Each seems important, and without a method the loudest one wins. Small teams then spend months on features that serve one person, while the thing most users struggle with stays broken.

Time is the scarce resource. A product with no roadmap tends to drift, and a team that cannot explain its priorities cannot say no politely.

## How planning improves the product and the team

A roadmap links effort to outcomes. Each item is tied to a goal, such as helping new users reach their first success or lowering support load, so you can judge afterwards whether it worked. Sorting ideas by value and by effort shows which are quick wins and which are expensive bets that need stronger evidence.

It also helps communication. A shareable roadmap lets a developer know what to start, a backer see where the product is heading and a customer understand why a request is not first in line. Dependencies and risks, once mapped, stop surprises such as a feature that cannot start until another is finished.

## What a good roadmap contains

- A short statement of the goals for the period ahead.
- Every idea collected in one list, with duplicates merged.
- Each item rated for value to users and to your business.
- A small, medium or large effort estimate for each item.
- A chosen order, with a written reason for each top pick.
- Three horizons: now, next and later.
- Success measures for each quarter, described in plain terms.
- Dependencies between items and the risks that could slow them.
- A clear list of ideas deliberately set aside.
- A one-page summary and, in larger packages, a shareable roadmap page.

## What we do

We begin with a planning call. Beforehand we ask for the feedback you have, any usage data and your goals for the next period. We read it, sort the ideas and propose an order, then discuss it with you and adjust.

The Basic package covers a short call, a sorted list of ideas, three chosen priorities and a one-page summary. Standard widens the list, builds a three-month plan with effort guesses and reviews your feedback and usage data. Premium covers six months in three horizons, goals per quarter, mapped dependencies, a shareable page and a follow-up call. A scoring sheet, an investor update draft and a quarterly refresh are available as extras. We do not commit to delivery dates for items.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Bring real feedback and usage data to the planning call.
- Link each item to a goal you can recognize afterwards.
- Leave room in the plan for fixes and surprises.
- Review the roadmap again when new evidence arrives.
- Say plainly what you are not building.

**Avoid:**
- Filling every week with new features.
- Letting one customer decide the order alone.
- Treating the roadmap as a promise to users.
- Planning too far ahead without evidence.
- Ignoring bugs and support work in the schedule.

## Who this service is for

Founders who launched and now feel pulled in many directions will gain focus. Small product teams without a dedicated manager can use it to agree an order of work. People preparing an update for investors or partners can show a reasoned plan rather than a wish list.

## What we need from you

A list of the ideas and requests you already have, your goals for the next few months, and any usage numbers, survey replies or support messages you can share. We use exports or a shared document, not your passwords. No product code access is required for this service.
